newsitem.title: USA: Clinton meets Kemp, fervent advocate of tax cuts.
newsitem.headline: Clinton meets Kemp, fervent advocate of tax cuts.

text.p: President Bill Clinton reached out to one of the country's most fervent advocates of tax cuts on Tuesday, meeting Republican Jack Kemp at the White House.

Kemp, a former U.S. football quarterback and congressman from New York, told reporters that he made his argument for tax cuts to the president in a 35-minute Oval Office meeting that included Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin.
In particular, Kemp said he pressed the Democratic president to cut the capital gains tax rate to 20 percent from 28 percent and to index this tax for inflation, a proposal Clinton opposes.

"The bottom line from me, of course, is not only permanent tax relief for families but cutting the capital gains tax rate down to 20 and indexing," Kemp, the 1996 Republican nominee for vice president, told reporters after the meeting.
Clinton in May reached a balanced-budget deal with the Republican-controlled Congress that aims to eliminate the federal deficit by 2002 while still cutting taxes by $85 billion over the period.
That agreement, however, left many details, including the exact structure of the tax cuts, to be decided by Congress.
The House and Senate, having each passed budget bills, are now hammering out their differences so that they can pass a "reconciliation" bill for the president's signature.
A White House official said that Kemp had requested the meeting with the president, adding that Clinton was interested in Kemp's ideas on a range of subjects, including taxes.
Kemp, a co-author of across-the-board tax cut legislation under former President Ronald Reagan, has long argued that lower taxes spur economic growth and lift government revenues.
